action-prediction.definition: Predicting the next UI action or action sequence from an instruction and the current screen.

automation.definition: Automating repetitive GUI tasks with scripts, programs, or agents.

cross-app.definition: Tasks that carry information or control across several applications or websites.

data-generation.definition: Collecting, synthesizing, or annotating screens, instructions, and trajectories for training or evaluation.

efficiency.definition: Reducing the latency, tokens, steps, or compute an agent needs to perceive, plan, or act.

evaluation.definition: Benchmarks, metrics, and evaluation methods for agents and their components.

grounding.definition: Locating the on-screen element or coordinates that an instruction refers to.

history.definition: Archived, legacy, or discontinued resources kept for historical context.

human-in-the-loop.definition: Agents that ask people, learn from them, or are corrected by them during a task.

imitation-learning.definition: Learning policies from human or synthetic demonstrations.

industry.definition: Companies, commercial deployments, and enterprise or industrial application domains.

interaction-history.definition: Using earlier screens, actions, or trajectories as context for the next decision.

long-horizon.definition: Tasks that need many dependent steps, subgoals, or long-term planning.

memory.definition: Storing and retrieving experience, app knowledge, or skills across steps or tasks.

observability.definition: Inspecting agent runs through traces, intermediate progress, failure analysis, and diagnostics.

planning.definition: Decomposing goals into subtasks and choosing action sequences.

recording.definition: Capturing human screen sessions, input events, or interaction traces.

reinforcement-learning.definition: Training agents from rewards with online or offline reinforcement learning.

reward-models.definition: Models or signals that score actions, steps, or outcomes for training or guidance.

robustness.definition: Reliability under perturbations, distribution shift, errors, or changing interfaces.

safety-security.definition: Attacks, defenses, privacy, policy compliance, and the risks of agent actions.

sandbox.definition: Isolated, reproducible environments such as virtual machines, emulators, and browsers for running agents.

science.definition: Agents for scientific, engineering, and data-science software.

screen-understanding.definition: Perceiving and describing interface layouts, elements, text, and structure.

self-reflection.definition: Agents that critique, verify, or revise their own actions and plans.

state-tracking.definition: Estimating and monitoring interface or task state, including whether an action took effect.

survey.definition: Literature surveys and overviews of the field.

tool-integration.definition: Combining GUI actions with APIs, code, terminals, or other tools.

training-free.definition: Improving agents through prompting or inference-time methods without training.

ui-design.definition: How interface design affects agents and users, and agents that evaluate or generate interfaces.

video.definition: Learning from, or evaluating on, screen recordings and tutorial videos.

web-navigation.definition: Operating websites and web applications in a browser.

workflow.definition: Multi-step procedures, business processes, and reusable task workflows.

world-models.definition: Predicting how an interface changes after an action, for planning or training.
